name: Nora Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me the public version and also what you really think. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Half my week I write production music, which is library music: short tracks that video makers, podcasters and small ad agencies license for their videos. I work from a box room in our flat with a keyboard, two speakers and a laptop, and I use AI every day for the boring bits, like cleaning stems and drafting the track descriptions. The other half I play synths in Glass Harbour, an indie band that gigs around the city most weekends, and I teach two online keyboard pupils. I'm honestly still a learner on the playing side; the band keeps me because I'm good with sounds, not because I'm fast.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does money look for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weirdly good for a musician my age. Three of my tracks got picked up by a big library and one ended up in a phone ad, so the royalties have been strong for two years. I've got about ten months of costs saved. Sam (my partner) is a software tester, so we split the rent on the flat near the canal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit. AI is a great assistant, it saves me an hour a day, and it was never going to write a song people love. I'd post that with a clip of the band.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased, because my setup works and the library money keeps coming. My real worry would still be the usual one: library tastes change fast, and my lucky ad money won't last forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep writing four or five library tracks a month and use the AI tools exactly as I do now. I'd spend some savings on a better synth for the band. And I'd keep pushing Glass Harbour to record an album this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. A bit restless, but that's just me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the ad money won't last. What's your plan for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to land a second ad, which is mostly luck and pitching. And I'd raise my online teaching to five pupils, because that's steady money that doesn't depend on a music supervisor liking my track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything worry you about Sam's work in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Sam (my partner) says the testing tools get a bit smarter every year, but the job's still there. If AI really did plateau, I think we'd both just carry on.

Raise online teaching to **five pupils** for steadier income.
feel: **Good**, though a bit restless, which she says is just her nature.

fieldNote: She uses AI daily and sees it as **a helper**, not a rival, in this world.

steps.text: Write four or five library tracks a month using current AI tools

Grow online keyboard teaching from two to five pupils

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say musicians should organise now: a collective licence so AI firms pay for the music they learned from, and a 'human-made' label buyers can trust. I'd post that and tag the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, library music is exactly what this world eats first. Video makers will generate a track for pennies, so library music rates fall through the floor. And Sam's job is testing software, which is also on the list, so both our incomes could shrink at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop writing generic tracks this winter and pitch custom scores directly to podcasters and small studios, using AI to work twice as fast. I'd help set up a co-op with four or five other library composers to sell human-made music together. And I'd push Glass Harbour to tour more, because live shows are the one thing a file can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired and a bit queasy. Part of me is excited to move first, part of me is watching our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Isn't that helping the thing you're worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I've thought about that a lot. If I don't use it, someone else does and undercuts me. I'd rather use it and fight for rules on who gets paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Sam (my partner) we should keep both our savings separate from day-to-day money and not touch them. Then we'd sit down and look at which of us is more likely to lose work first. I genuinely don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a political emergency, not a tech story. AI companies should pay a big share of what they earn into a fund for the people they replace, and I'd march for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my library and custom work is dead by 2028. It's all screens and files, the first thing AGI does. Live gigs with Glass Harbour carry on until robots can play in 2031, so that's where my income has to go, fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend this year turning Glass Harbour into a proper live act, with more shows and merch. I'd use AI to run the band's booking and social media so we can play twice as many gigs. I'd also learn live sound, because someone has to run the desk at small venues until the robots come, and Sam and I would save hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly, with a lot of adrenaline on top. I'd be busy, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the gap between 2028 and 2031 mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's three years where being in a room with people is worth something. I'd squeeze every gig out of it. But I know my playing isn't good enough yet to stand out once everyone else rushes to live work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you put the blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly on the companies and on governments that let them move this fast with no plan. Musicians didn't ask for AGI. Ordinary people never get a vote on the speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set up proper rules if we start this year. I'd keep pushing the co-op and the collective licence, loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I can ride the next three or four years of library work with AI doing most of the grind, while I build the live side. By 2031 I'd want the band to be my main income and my playing to be properly good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI to triple my library output now and bank the extra, while rates are still decent. I'd take keyboard lessons with a jazz pianist every week to fix my weak playing. And I'd put money into a small van for the band, so we can tour without hiring one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a useful way. It gives me a to-do list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tripling your output, isn't that just speeding up the fall in rates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a little, yes. Everyone will do the same. But I'd rather bank the money while library rates are still there than be the last one making tracks by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to Sam's job in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam (my partner) would probably have a couple more years than me, then the same problem. We've talked about Sam training as a nurse, which needs hands and people. It's a real conversation now, not a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade to build something fair: co-ops, licences, a fund for musicians. That's my public line and I mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is a lot for me. I can become a properly good player and build the band into something real. I'd also expect new jobs I can't picture yet, like directing AI music for films.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing library work with AI for as long as it pays and save half of it. I'd start a small online course teaching other composers how to use AI tools, since I'm good at that. And I'd want the co-op running with twenty members by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but mostly hopeful. There's room to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said new jobs might appear. Is that wishful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit. But every big change in music made new jobs, like producers when tape came along. I'd bet on being early to whatever it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have done by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A band people pay to see, a co-op that pays fair rates, and a pile of savings. If I had those three things, I think I'd face the robots in 2039 feeling okay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Sam and I both work at screens and both incomes would go in the same couple of years. What would help is a fund paid by AI companies that covers retraining, like Sam's nursing course, and a collective licence so musicians get paid for what was learned from them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about money versus love, which is the real question for musicians. I'd still make music every day if nobody paid for it. The question is whether I'd need a second job to pay the rent.

headlineQuote: I'd still make music every day if nobody paid for it. The question is whether I'd need a second job to pay the rent.
portrait: Nora is a 27-year-old **library composer** and synth player in the indie band Glass Harbour.
She uses AI **every day** and has ten months saved from lucky ad royalties.
Her partner Sam's **software testing** job is also exposed, doubling household risk.
She moves first in every scenario: **co-op**, custom work, touring and teaching AI.
She wants AI firms to pay through **collective licences** and a retraining fund.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both her and Sam's screen-based incomes would go together.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining fund** paid by AI companies, covering courses like Sam's nursing.
A **collective licence** so musicians are paid for what AI learned from them.
